Where it began

Jacques Kallis was born in Pinelands on 16 October 1975, and learned his cricket at Wynberg Boys' High School. The school thought enough of him to name its main ground after him in 2009. He played first-class cricket for Western Province B at 18, and that English summer he played club cricket in Solihull, where the coaches spotted a future all-rounder. A year later, at Netherfield in Kendal, he made 791 runs in 14 games.

The player

His Test debut came against England at Durban in December 1995. The first few matches were hard going, but in 1997 he batted through to save a Test at Melbourne with a hundred, and from then on he was a fixture. By late 2001 he was the top-ranked Test all-rounder in the world.

In 166 Tests between 1995 and 2013 he made 13,289 runs at 55.37, with 45 hundreds and a best of 224 against Sri Lanka at Newlands. He also took 292 wickets at 32.65 and held 198 catches. By November 2026 he ranked fourth of all Test cricketers on our figures for runs and second for hundreds. Twice he made hundreds in four Tests in a row, and in his last Test, at Durban in December 2013, he signed off with one more. He won 23 player-of-the-match awards in Tests, and by November 2026 nobody had won more.

What made him special

He was two cricketers for the price of one. Settled at number three, he batted with a textbook defence, a lovely cover drive and a rare sense of when to dig in and when to push on. With the ball he swung it at a lively pace and had a habit of taking the wicket that mattered. Very few Test all-rounders have finished with a batting average 20 or more above their bowling average, and he is one of them, alongside Garry Sobers and Wally Hammond.

If there was a gentle grumble, it was that he could have changed gear a little sooner. He tended to reply that South Africa won more often when he stayed in, and the scorebook rather backs him up.

Away from the middle

He was the ICC's Cricketer of the Year in 2005, sharing the Sobers Trophy with Andrew Flintoff, and Wisden made him its Leading Cricketer in the World for 2007 and a Cricketer of the Year in 2013. South Africa gave him the Order of Ikhamanga in Silver, and in 2020 he entered the ICC Hall of Fame. After playing he coached Kolkata Knight Riders and advised the batters of South Africa and England. His scholarship foundation gives talented youngsters money and mentoring so they can do well at both sport and their studies.

And finally

At 47 he turned out in a masters T10 match in the United States and made an unbeaten 64 off 31 balls. For a man who liked to take his time, it was a cheerful last word.
